source.title: Can Stability be Detrimental? Better Generalization through Gradient Descent Instabilities

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own experiments on learning-rate choices and generalization, and correlations between measured properties and validation performance. These use different measures and interventions from the listed versions.
record.gate_note: Results cited from prior work are not included. The paper's own validation-accuracy comparisons and metric correlations are included. Values shown only in Figures 5 and 6 are recorded as figure-only; no precise values are inferred from the plots.
record.test_reason: The study tests learning-rate-induced instability and generalization, but none of V1–V8. Its sharpness measure is the unnormalized largest Hessian eigenvalue, not V7's magnitude-aware weight-perturbation measure. It also does not compare sharpness with norm- and margin-based measures. Full-batch training without a batch-size comparison does not test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that sufficiently large learning rates induce instabilities favoring flatter regions and improved generalization, and propose Hessian eigenvector rotations as the mechanism. Their suggestion that rotations can predict generalization better than Hessian sharpness is preliminary; experiments use full-batch gradient descent, with extension to stochastic training left open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies learning-rate-induced instability, Hessian eigenvector rotation, and generalization correlations. Its experiments use full-batch gradient descent, often without explicit regularization; this does not reproduce the specific methods in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization gains depend on learning rate: they emerge beyond the stability threshold, eventually fall at excessive rates, and vary by dataset. Results also vary with when the learning rate is reduced; metric correlations differ between constant-rate and reduction settings, and by whether the learning rate is controlled.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation accuracy improves beyond the measured stability threshold on fMNIST and CIFAR10-5k, then falls at excessive learning rates. Full-dataset results also generally improve with larger learning rates, without measured stability thresholds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-divergent large learning rates can improve generalization in full-batch gradient descent, with a useful range that depends on the task.

fits_no_version.finding: Longer exposure to large initial learning rates reduces eventual Hessian sharpness; on CIFAR10-5k, most models also improve validation performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Longer training with instability-inducing learning rates can progressively flatten the loss landscape and improve generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Tabulated ResNet20 learning-rate reductions lower validation accuracy relative to corresponding constant-rate runs. The paper gives conflicting final learning rates in the text and caption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization benefit of learning-rate reduction depends on its timing and training regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Learning rate, unnormalized Hessian sharpness, and eigenvector similarity correlate with validation performance across learning-rate sweeps. Controlling learning rate changes these associations; the authors characterize the initialization-controlled evidence as inconclusive.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Associations of Hessian sharpness and eigenvector similarity with generalization depend on whether learning rate varies across models.

record.code_released: The code for reproducing the experiments and results in this paper will be made available on GitHub upon publication.
record.problems: The CIFAR10-5k experiments use a reduced 10% subset. The controlled-learning-rate metric comparison uses sets of nine models and is described as inconclusive due to small sample size. The authors say stability limits were not computed for the full-dataset experiments. Generalization results use validation performance and the models are trained to > 99.99% training accuracy. The study is fully non-stochastic and calls for future work on stochastic gradient descent.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported result rows were left out. The paper also reports training-loss, sharpness, parameter-oscillation, and eigenvector-rotation dynamics; these do not directly report the generalization outcomes or metrics relevant to the cataloged versions and are not included.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out performance compared with natural-label generalization.
Width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks on matched image tasks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V8. Failure of unnormalized Hessian sharpness to predict generalization does not challenge V7's magnitude-aware measure. Figure 7 additionally reports learning-rate-3.2 reduction results of 84.98% and 86.92%, versus 87.32% without reduction; these omitted values concern no listed version and therefore are not missing claim evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Large-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.
